deep.heading: How iRacing reads the two pictures
deep.body: iRacing gets two pictures for your car. The paint picture is the colour you see. The spec picture is four numbers per pixel that tell the lighting engine what the surface is made of: red is metal, green is roughness, blue is the clear layer on top, alpha is a lighting mask. The sim lights every pixel from those four numbers, using its sun, sky and your view angle. That is why the same paint can look like wet enamel, brushed steel or flat vinyl without a single colour changing.

deep.heading: Why paint and spec are never judged apart
deep.body: Metal reflection is tinted by the paint colour, while clear-coat highlights are close to white. So a metal value of 255 on a near-white paint gives silver, the same value on a dark red gives dark tinted metal, and on near-black it can vanish. The spec only decides how much of each effect you get. The colour you painted decides what that effect looks like. Judge the two together, on the car, never one without the other.

deep.heading: What Shokker Paint Booth does for you
deep.body: You never paint these four numbers by hand. Every zone has a base finish that sets a starting metal, roughness and coat, then pattern, overlays and sliders move them. At the very end the app raises any coat value below 16 to 16 and any roughness below 15 to 15 unless the pixel is chrome tier (metal 240 or more), so a render cannot hand iRacing a value that whitewashes. The paint goes out as a 24-bit picture and the spec as a 32-bit picture with alpha, both for the same car.

examples.title: Same red, three materials
examples.goal: See that one colour becomes three looks through spec alone.
examples.result: Gel Coat is a wet-looking red, Clear Satin is a soft low-sheen red, and Chrome turns the red into tinted mirror metal. The paint picture is identical in all three.

examples.title: Read a spec colour at a glance
examples.goal: Tell what a spec picture colour means before opening any tool.

settings.White: rough metal with the coat off, not chrome

examples.result: You can sort a whole spec picture into gloss, chrome, matte and rough metal just by its colour families.

combos.why: Teaches the colour code of a spec picture so you can read any export.
The three limits applied to every render, and why they exist.
How to choose paint and spec so they help each other.

faq.q: Do I have to understand the spec map to use the app?
faq.a: No. Pick a finish and the app sets all four numbers. Read this when you want to tune a shine, fix a washed-out look or build your own material.

faq.q: Does the spec map change how the car drives?
faq.a: No. Spec only changes how the car looks, never how it handles.

faq.q: What happens if there is no spec file?
faq.a: iRacing falls back to the car's normal material and your colours still show. You just lose your custom shine.

faq.q: Why does iRacing look different from the preview?
faq.a: The preview is a quick design view. iRacing lights the real render with its own sun, shadows and materials, and it reads the spec file separately, so shine only shows in the sim.

mistakes.symptom: The finish looks washed out and white in the sim.
mistakes.cause: A clear-coat value between 1 and 15 reached iRacing. That band is treated as no coat or a legacy value.
mistakes.fix: Re-render from the app instead of editing the file by hand. The app raises every coat value to at least 16.

mistakes.symptom: Silver chrome comes out black or grey.
mistakes.cause: Metal reflection takes the paint colour, and the paint under it was dark or mid grey.
mistakes.fix: Paint the zone near-white, or use a Foundation chrome with Use source paint if you want to keep your colours and accept tinted chrome.

mistakes.symptom: I changed a spec value and nothing happened.
mistakes.cause: The old compiled copy of the spec is still loaded by the sim.
mistakes.fix: Render again, then press Ctrl+R in iRacing. If it still looks old, move the compiled spec copy for that car out of the folder and reload.

protips: The preview shows the same colours as the render but not the same shine, so judge shine on the spec views (R METAL, G ROUGH, B COAT) and in the sim.
A dark paint under high metal is buried: nearly black until the right reflection arrives. Colour first, then metal.

deep.heading: The six metal bands
deep.body: 0 to 15 is plain non-metal: enamel, lacquer, rubber, glass. 16 to 63 is low metal such as carbon, mineral loading or subtle flake. 64 to 127 is pearl, mica and patina. 128 to 175 is strong pearl or anodized metal. 176 to 239 is true metallic: aluminium, gunmetal, brushed titanium, metallic candy. 240 to 255 is chrome tier, the only band allowed to push roughness below 15. Foundation anchors: Pearl 100, Metallic 200, Candy 200, Satin Chrome 250, Chrome 255.

deep.heading: Metal eats the paint colour
deep.body: As metal goes up, the surface shows less of its own diffuse colour and more of a tinted reflection. Past about 240 almost everything you see is reflection, tinted by the paint colour. That is why silver chrome needs near-white paint and why a fully metallic dark red looks nearly black. Partial-metal finishes such as pearl, metallic and satin chrome keep their colour much better than full chrome.

deep.heading: What moves metal after the base
deep.body: Spec Strength pulls metal toward zero: metal becomes metal times strength, so 50 percent of Chrome is about 128. The R METAL slider adds a value from minus 127 to plus 127 under the zone mask and clips at 0 and 255. Spec patterns add their pattern to metal when the M tick is on. After those, the Material Remap tool squeezes metal into a new low-to-high range and the Material Override tool can set it flat, so those two can overrule the slider.

examples.title: Pearl that shimmers but keeps its colour
examples.goal: Get depth without losing the paint colour.
examples.result: A soft pearl shimmer that sits on your own colours, about a third of full metal.

examples.title: Gunmetal sheen on a dark car
examples.goal: Make a dark car read as metal, not as black paint.
examples.result: Dark paint with a real metallic sparkle in sun. Going all the way to 255 would bury the colour instead.

combos.why: Metal says what it is, roughness says how sharp it reflects. Always set them as a pair.
Shows where every metal and roughness pair lands as a material.
Where the R METAL nudge fits in the order of operations.

faq.q: What is the best metal value for chrome?
faq.a: 255. The Foundation Chrome uses metal 255, roughness 2, coat 16. Anything from 240 up is chrome tier.

faq.q: Why is my metallic car dark?
faq.a: Metal reflection inherits the paint colour. Dark paint plus high metal is buried until light hits it. Lower metal to around 180 to 200, or lighten the paint.

faq.q: Is more metal always shinier?
faq.a: No. Shine is mostly roughness. Metal controls what the reflection is made of. A rough, metallic surface is satin or brushed, not shiny.

faq.q: What metal do pearl and candy use?
faq.a: Pearl is 100. Candy is 200 in the current registry, with a low roughness of 15 so the tinted coat reads deep.

mistakes.symptom: Gloss black turned into dark metal.
mistakes.cause: Metal was raised, by a slider, a metallic overlay or a wrong base.
mistakes.fix: Keep metal at 0 with a wet-look gloss such as Gel Coat 0, 15, 16 or Gloss 0, 30, 16.

mistakes.symptom: Coloured chrome looks muddy.
mistakes.cause: A dark, over-saturated paint is under the metal and buries the reflection.
mistakes.fix: Use a bright, controlled colour of the same hue under chrome or candy.

mistakes.symptom: Metal slider seems to stop working.
mistakes.cause: It was already at 0 or 255, where the result is clipped.
mistakes.fix: Move the other way, or change the base so there is room above or below.

protips: Metal bands decide the legal roughness: only metal 240 or more may have roughness under 15. A chrome-tier pixel is the one place a mirror is allowed.
Spec Strength is the quick way to get half-metal: 50 percent strength on Chrome gives about 128, a pearl-level metal, without picking another finish.

deep.heading: Nine roughness bands
deep.body: 0 to 14 razor mirror, reserved for chrome-tier pixels. 15 to 29 wet gloss. 30 to 59 high gloss. 60 to 99 satin gloss. 100 to 129 satin or eggshell. 130 to 159 semi-matte. 160 to 199 matte or blasted. 200 to 229 flat. 230 to 255 dead or porous. Anchors: Gel Coat 15, Gloss 30, Semi Gloss 55, Satin 95, Eggshell 140, Matte 200, Primer 215, Flat Black 250.

deep.heading: The floor of 15 and the chrome exception
deep.body: Roughness below 15 is reserved for mirror metal, so every render lifts it to 15 wherever metal is under 240. Chrome-tier pixels, metal 240 or more, keep their low values: Foundation Chrome is roughness 2. Pixels that come from a pattern whose own spec amount is on are exempt from this floor.

deep.heading: Smooth ramps smear, steps travel
deep.body: A continuous high-roughness gradient makes the highlight smear across the panel. Quantised roughness steps make the highlight jump in controlled stages as the camera moves, which is how engineered finishes get a sparkle that travels. Spec Strength pivots roughness around 128: roughness becomes 128 plus (roughness minus 128) times strength, so strength 0 gives a neutral 128.

examples.title: Make a car less shiny without changing colour
examples.goal: Tame a too-glossy zone.
examples.result: Roughness rises by 40 so reflections soften. Either control works; the slider adds, the strength pulls toward 128.

examples.title: Satin from gloss
examples.goal: Move from a wet look to a quiet satin.
examples.result: The same colours with a low sheen that hides small flaws.

combos.why: Roughness and coat together make satin versus matte. Raising roughness alone leaves a glossy halo.
G ROUGH is added after patterns and before remap, and is clipped at 15.
The floor of 15 and the chrome exception in one place.

faq.q: What roughness is a mirror?
faq.a: 0 on paper, but only chrome-tier pixels (metal 240 or more) may go under 15. Foundation Chrome uses 2.

faq.q: Why can I not go below 15 on a gloss car?
faq.a: The app lifts non-chrome roughness to 15 on every render because lower values flare badly in the sim.

faq.q: Which is better for matte, roughness or coat?
faq.a: Both. Matte colour is roughly roughness 200 and coat 160, for example. Do not use alpha to fake matte.

faq.q: Does roughness change the colour?
faq.a: Not directly. It changes how wide and bright the reflection is, which can make a colour look lighter or deeper.

mistakes.symptom: Matte paint still has a glossy halo.
mistakes.cause: Roughness was raised but the clearcoat byte was left at 16, so a sharp coat layer sits over a rough base.
mistakes.fix: Raise coat to around 160 as well, or start from Soft Matte (0, 200, 165).

mistakes.symptom: Highlight smears into one large blur.
mistakes.cause: A smooth roughness gradient across the panel.
mistakes.fix: Use a few distinct roughness steps, or a spec pattern, so the highlight moves in controlled jumps.

mistakes.symptom: Mirror finish looks dull.
mistakes.cause: Roughness above 15 on a metal 255 surface, or coat byte high.
mistakes.fix: Start from Chrome (255, 2, 16) and check the B COAT view is dark green-blue, not bright.

protips: Satin is not one number. Eggshell sits at roughness 140, Satin at 95 and Semi Gloss at 55. Pick the base that matches the look instead of dialling roughness blind.
Wet droplets look: base 0, 22, 16 with rims at roughness 15 and the lens at 35 to 70, in 8 to 24 pixel drops.

deep.heading: The backwards channel in full
deep.body: Blue 16 is the strongest active coat. Values rise toward 255 as the coat fades: 17 to 31 very strong, 32 to 63 strong to medium, 64 to 127 satin, 128 to 191 dull, 192 to 254 almost none, 255 none. Values 0 to 15 are treated by the sim as no coat or a legacy value. 255 is the raw maximum byte but the weakest clearcoat. Old notes that call it maximum are wrong.

deep.heading: The floor of 16 and its two exceptions
deep.body: In a normal render every coat value is raised to at least 16, including matte, so no pixel lands in the 1 to 15 band that whitewashes. The two exceptions are pixels from an imported spec (including the SHOKK DROP authored sets) and pixels where a pattern spec amount is on; those keep their exact values, 0 included. Resizing or smoothing a spec picture can create 1 to 15 values by accident, which is another reason to re-render instead of resizing.

deep.heading: Clearcoat quality and strength
deep.body: The quality control maps straight onto the byte: coat = 16 + (1 minus quality) times 239. Quality 1.0 is coat 16, quality 0.5 is about 135, quality 0 is 255. Spec Strength pulls coat toward 16: coat becomes 16 + (coat minus 16) times strength, so strength 0 gives the full glossy 16. Never blend a coat value from 0 to 16 across an edge; the blend passes through the dead 1 to 15 band. Use a hard edge or blend from 16 upward.

examples.title: Candy depth
examples.goal: A deep wet colour on a metallic body.
examples.result: Maximum coat on a tinted base, which is what makes candy look bottomless.

examples.title: Soft matte without glare
examples.goal: A flat stealth finish that does not shine at an angle.
examples.result: Roughness and coat are both high so no wet halo appears. Pushing coat up further removes the last bit of sheen.

combos.why: The pair that separates satin from matte.
Why the coat floor is 16 and where the exceptions are.
The Spec Sculpt Lab applies the same floor to every file it writes.

faq.q: Is a bigger blue number more clearcoat?
faq.a: No. It is the reverse. 16 is the strongest coat and 255 is none.

faq.q: Why does the app raise my coat 0 to 16?
faq.a: Values 1 to 15 whitewash in the sim and exact 0 means coat disabled, which in normal renders is also raised to 16. Only imported specs and pattern-driven pixels may keep 0.

faq.q: What coat do Foundation finishes use?
faq.a: Gloss and Wet Look 16, Pearl 16, Metallic 16, Chrome 16, Candy 16, Satin Chrome 40, Clear Satin 75, Brushed 65, Soft Matte 165.

faq.q: Can I make blue 255 for a matte look?
faq.a: Only with an imported or authored spec. In normal zones values from 192 to 254 give almost-no coat and are the usual matte territory.

mistakes.symptom: Chrome is dull even on white paint.
mistakes.cause: The coat byte is high, for example 255, which removes the coat reflectivity.
mistakes.fix: Use coat 16 on chrome. Check the B COAT view is dark.

mistakes.symptom: A fade between a clear zone and a bare zone looks whitewashed in the middle.
mistakes.cause: The blend passed through coat 1 to 15.
mistakes.fix: Use a hard edge, or keep both sides at 16 or more.

mistakes.symptom: A slider made the coat go the wrong way.
mistakes.cause: B COAT is added straight to the value, so plus means duller.
mistakes.fix: Move B COAT left for glossier, right for duller. Nothing goes under 16.

protips: Offsetting the coat structure a little from the metal and roughness structure gives a depth cue, because the two highlight lobes peak at different angles.
Clear Satin is only 75 on blue but 100 on green. Many satin looks are about roughness. Coat is what makes the edge of a highlight crisp or soft.

deep.heading: What alpha really does
deep.body: Alpha is a lighting and specular mask, not opacity and not a matte switch. 255 means full normal lighting, which is the production default and what every normal zone has. 128 reduces the response and is only meant for specialised fake-depth or shadow tricks. 0 kills lighting and specular response completely, useful for faked vents or unlit holes, but a flat sticker look if overused.

deep.heading: Where alpha comes from in a render
deep.body: The spec starts with alpha 255 everywhere. The only things that change it are the Lighting Mask tool, the Material Override tool (when it sets alpha) and an imported spec map. Soft zone edges also blend alpha across the border, so a soft edge gives a soft lighting fade. The Lighting Mask runs together with the other spec tools after the sliders and before the final coat and roughness floors.

deep.heading: Matte is not alpha
deep.body: A common mistake is lowering alpha to get a matte colour. Matte comes from higher roughness and higher clearcoat bytes (for example 0, 200, 160). Reducing alpha only mutes lighting and makes the area look dead and flat, as if it were printed on.

examples.title: Fake grille holes
examples.goal: Make a printed grille look like dark openings.
examples.result: The grille loses all reflection and reads as a dark gap. Use it on small areas only.

examples.title: Subtle depth in a recessed panel
examples.goal: Reduce highlights in a recess without going fully dark.
examples.result: Lighting response is reduced there, so the panel reads as recessed.

combos.why: The three power tools, with Lighting Mask as the one that touches alpha.
Alpha is the one channel the floors do not touch.

faq.q: Should I touch alpha for a normal car?
faq.a: No. Keep it at 255. The app does that for you.

faq.q: Can alpha make a hole in the car?
faq.a: It can fake one for lighting, but it does not change the car shape or the paint.

faq.q: Why does my matte look flat and dead?
faq.a: If alpha was lowered, the lighting response is gone. Reset to 255 and use roughness and coat for matte.

faq.q: Does soft edge affect alpha?
faq.a: Yes. Soft edges blend alpha as well as colour, so a lighting mask fades softly at its border.

mistakes.symptom: A zone looks like a flat sticker on track.
mistakes.cause: Alpha is at or near 0 over a large area.
mistakes.fix: Set the Lighting Mask back to Full Lighting A255, or Use Source Alpha.

mistakes.symptom: Matte colour is not matte.
mistakes.cause: Reduced alpha was used as the matte control.
mistakes.fix: Raise roughness and coat bytes instead, for example start from Soft Matte.

protips: Use Source Alpha in the Lighting Mask tool keeps whatever alpha the zone already has, so it is the no-change choice.
Set a lighting mask only after you are happy with metal, roughness and coat, because it hides their effect where it applies.

deep.heading: Why spec pictures use odd colours
deep.body: The spec picture is data, not paint. Red holds metal, green holds roughness, blue holds the clear coat, so every colour is a code. Bright green does not mean glossy, it means very rough and matte. Bright blue means a weak clear coat, not the strongest one. Red alone means metal. Yellow, red plus green, is rough metal. White is rough metal with the coat off, which is not chrome and not gloss.

deep.heading: The neighbourhoods worth memorising
deep.body: A dark green-black such as 0, 30, 16 is the normal gloss neighbourhood. Bright red such as 255, 2, 16 is the chrome neighbourhood. Pure green 0, 255, 0 is dead matte. 255, 255, 0 is chalky or oxidised raw metal. Magenta, 255, 0, 255, is mirror metal with the coat suppressed, an extreme corner used by Fractured night carriers, not ordinary gloss.

deep.heading: A trap in the preview
deep.body: The colour views under the live preview show bytes, not a paint job. A hot-pink spec region is just the way high metal, a high coat byte and low roughness pack into colour. On its own it does nothing; the effect needs spatial pattern, crushed dark paint and lighting around it.

examples.title: Reading a gloss car
examples.goal: Confirm a gloss body is healthy.
examples.result: Metal 0, roughness about 30, coat 16: wet-looking paint with no metal.

examples.title: Reading chrome trim
examples.goal: Confirm chrome parts are set up for a mirror.
examples.result: Metal 255, roughness 2, coat 16: a mirror.

combos.why: Click a spot and read the exact bytes instead of guessing from colour.
Blue is backwards; the most common mis-reading.

faq.q: Why is my gloss car green in the spec view?
faq.a: Dark green-black is the code for normal gloss. The green is the roughness byte, around 30.

faq.q: What colour is chrome in a spec picture?
faq.a: Bright red, because metal is 255 and the green and blue bytes are low.

faq.q: What does white mean?
faq.a: Rough metal with the coat off. It is not chrome.

faq.q: Is the spec picture what iRacing shows?
faq.a: No. iRacing reads the numbers and lights the car with them. The picture is only for you.

mistakes.symptom: I thought bright green meant glossy.
mistakes.cause: Green is roughness, so bright green is very rough.
mistakes.fix: Look for dark green or black for gloss. Use the G ROUGH view to confirm.

mistakes.symptom: I thought bright blue meant maximum coat.
mistakes.cause: Blue is backwards: 16 is the strongest coat and bright blue is a weak coat.
mistakes.fix: The strongest coat is a dark blue channel. Check B COAT.

protips: Switch to the single-channel views (R METAL, G ROUGH, B COAT) when something looks wrong. The mixed colour hides which channel is off.
Use the Channels readout to see exact numbers before changing any slider.

deep.heading: Every finish has a home on the grid
deep.body: Put metal across and roughness down. Low metal with low roughness (0 and 15 to 30) is wet paint and gel coat. Low metal with high roughness (0 and 200 or more) is matte and flat. High metal with low roughness (250 or more and 2 to 15) is chrome. High metal with high roughness (180 and 160) is bead blast and sandblasted metal. The middle band is where brushed, pearl and satin chrome live. The coat then adds the polish on top.

deep.heading: Anchor cards with exact values
deep.body: Liquid glaze 0, 15, 16. Wet look 0, 22, 16. Gloss 0, 30, 16. Semi gloss 0, 55, 40. Satin 0, 95, 70. Eggshell 0, 140, 100. Matte 0, 200, 160. Flat black 0, 250, 255. Pearl 100, 40, 16. Metallic 200, 50, 16. Gunmetal 220, 40, 16. Brushed titanium 180, 70, 16. Antique chrome 220, 18, 50. Dark chrome 250, 15, 40. Chrome 255, 2, 16. Satin chrome 250, 45, 40. Candy 200, 15, 16. Gloss carbon 55, 30, 16. Satin carbon 55, 110, 120.

deep.heading: Live finishes move around their anchor
deep.body: Real finishes are not one point. Chrome is 245 plus 10 times a displacement for metal and 2 plus 8 times it for roughness. Dark chrome is 230 plus 20 times a field. Metallic flake is 168 plus up to 24 from the body and 14 from the polish. Pearl layers sit at metal 90 plus 55 times a layer. Quantised steps are what make highlights jump instead of smearing.

examples.title: Pick a point, then pick the finish
examples.goal: Choose a Foundation finish from where you want it on the grid.
examples.result: Four corners of the grid in four clicks, all keeping your paint colours.

examples.title: Mix two corners on one car
examples.goal: Get the matte-beside-metal contrast that makes a livery pop.
examples.result: Two materials from opposite sides of the grid, with a clean edge between them.

combos.why: Which corner of the grid suits which paint colour.
The Foundation shelf is the grid, one finish per useful point.

faq.q: Where does satin chrome sit?
faq.a: Near metal 250, roughness 45, coat 40: metal like chrome but with soft reflections.

faq.q: What separates pearl from metallic?
faq.a: Metal. Pearl is about 100, metallic about 200.

faq.q: Where is carbon?
faq.a: Low metal, 55, with a gloss roughness of 30 or satin 110. The weave itself comes from a pattern.

faq.q: Why are there matte metals?
faq.a: Metal and roughness are independent. Matte metallic is 225, 140, 100 and bead blast is 180, 160, 140.

mistakes.symptom: My brushed look is just a flat grey metal.
mistakes.cause: Only the average values were set. Brushed needs variation in the spec.
mistakes.fix: Add a brushed spec overlay on top of Brushed 180, 75, 65.

mistakes.symptom: A roughness under 15 was changed back.
mistakes.cause: It was a non-chrome pixel, so the floor lifted it.
mistakes.fix: Raise metal to 240 or more if you want a true mirror.

protips: The grid is two-dimensional but a good finish uses a third dimension: variation. Flat points look like paint swatches, varied points look like materials.
Dark chrome (250, 15, 40) is the quickest way to a black mirror finish; the extra coat makes it less sharp than chrome.

deep.heading: The exact rules and the numbers behind them
deep.body: Rule one, coat: every coat value is raised to at least 16 (the app calls this the clearcoat floor). Rule two, roughness: wherever metal is under 240, roughness is raised to at least 15. Metal of 240 or more is chrome tier and may keep roughness down to 0. Rule three, alpha: it starts at 255 everywhere and only a lighting mask, an override or an imported spec changes it. After the rules, values are clipped to 0 to 255 and any invalid number becomes a safe value. These run at the very end of a render, so no slider, overlay or tool can slip past them.

deep.heading: Why each rule exists
deep.body: Coat values 1 to 15 sit in the band the sim reads as no coat or legacy, and they whitewash the paint; resizing or smoothing a spec file creates them by accident, so the app removes the whole band. Roughness under 15 is reserved for mirror metal, so a gloss or satin zone is held at 15 and only a chrome-tier pixel can be a true mirror. Alpha stays at full lighting because it is a mask for the lighting response, not a gloss control; dropping it makes an area look dead.

deep.heading: The two places a value may stay below the floor
deep.body: Pixels from an imported or authored spec (the SHOKK DROP sets) keep their exact coat. Pixels from a pattern whose own spec amount is switched on are also left alone, because the pattern carries its own material. Everything else is lifted. If a design truly needs exact no-coat, check the exported file with the Inspector instead of trusting the preview.

examples.title: The slider that stops
examples.goal: Understand why B COAT will not go glossier than 16.
examples.result: The result is clipped at 16. Nothing changes, because 16 is already the glossiest coat the app allows.

examples.title: Roughness cannot go under 15
examples.goal: See the roughness floor on a non-metal finish.
examples.result: Roughness stays at 15 because the pixel is not chrome tier. Only metal of 240 or more may go lower.

combos.why: The blue channel details behind rule one.
The Spec Sculpt Lab applies the same rules before it writes a file.
Slider shifts are clipped at 0, 15 and 16 before the final rules run.

faq.q: Can I turn the iron rules off?
faq.a: No. They protect every file from values that look wrong in the sim.

faq.q: Why is my chrome allowed roughness 2 but my gloss is not?
faq.a: Only pixels with metal of 240 or more may go below 15. Gloss has metal 0, so it is held at 15.

faq.q: Does a hand-edited spec file get checked?
faq.a: Only if you bring it back into the app as an imported spec. Files you edit elsewhere are your responsibility.

faq.q: Does the preview follow the same rules?
faq.a: Yes. The preview runs the same final rules as the export.

mistakes.symptom: My exact coat of 0 became 16.
mistakes.cause: Normal zones are floored at 16. Only imported specs and pattern-driven pixels keep 0.
mistakes.fix: Use coat 16 for the shiniest look, or import an authored spec if you really need coat off.

mistakes.symptom: A blend between a clear zone and a bare zone looks whitewashed.
mistakes.cause: The blend crossed coat 1 to 15.
mistakes.fix: Hard-edge the zone, or keep both sides at 16 or more.

mistakes.symptom: A roughness below 15 got lifted.
mistakes.cause: The pixel is not chrome tier.
mistakes.fix: Raise metal to 240 or more if you want a mirror there.

protips: The iron rules are a safety net, not a design tool. If a slider hits one, the look is telling you to change the base finish instead.
Resizing a spec picture in an editor can reintroduce illegal values. Re-render at 2048 instead.

deep.heading: What actually makes a finish pop
deep.body: Saturation alone does not pop. Complementary neighbour contrast does: deep blue beside warm gold, black beside hot pink, white beside red. Then make the spec the colour-opposite of the paint: a warm paint on matte next to a cool colour on metal reads richer than one shine everywhere. Adjacent areas should differ in colour or in shine, ideally both. One loud hero area (hood or a big panel), calm neighbours, and fine texture for depth, not big blobs.

deep.heading: Paint guidance by material
deep.body: Silver chrome: near-white neutral paint. Coloured chrome or candy: a bright, controlled colour, since an over-saturated dark paint buries the mirror. Pearl: body hue plus lighter and darker flake colours, because a uniform paint makes the spec look pasted on. Gloss black: near-black paint with metal kept at 0. Matte colour: a normal body hue with roughness and coat raised, never reduced alpha. Weathering: oxide colours lined up with the worn spec.

deep.heading: A palette that reads as expensive
deep.body: Two or three colours plus one accent looks expensive; five looks cheap. A good split is about 60 percent dominant, 30 percent accent, 10 percent trim. Candy, pearl, metallic, satin or gloss in the livery colour read premium on big areas; chrome on a large area is loud and shows every flaw, so use it on accents, trim and thin lines. A chrome pinstripe on a matte car reads as real chrome.

examples.title: Two-material hood
examples.goal: Make the hood the hero without a new colour.
examples.result: Glossy candy hood, flat neighbours and a bright satin accent: three surfaces, one palette.

examples.title: Stealth with one accent
examples.goal: A dark car that still has life.
examples.result: The matte body hides panel lines, the satin accent gives a quiet edge, and the numbers stay readable.

combos.why: The livery view of the same idea, with zone roles.
Pick the two opposite corners for your neighbouring zones.
Neighbouring zones only show contrast if the right zone owns the shared edge.

faq.q: Why does my bright colour look flat?
faq.a: Probably the shine is the same everywhere. Add a neighbour with the opposite shine.

faq.q: Does more saturation help?
faq.a: No. Contrast between neighbours helps. More saturation mostly muddies a spec.

faq.q: What goes behind numbers?
faq.a: A calm gloss, satin or matte with strong colour contrast. Avoid sparkle, strong patterns and colour-shifting finishes there.

faq.q: Chrome on the whole car?
faq.a: It is loud and shows every flaw. It works as a show-car statement, but accents and trim usually look better.

mistakes.symptom: Everything is metallic and nothing stands out.
mistakes.cause: One shine used all over.
mistakes.fix: Choose a hero zone, then give the neighbours matte or satin.

mistakes.symptom: Black chrome looks like a black hole.
mistakes.cause: Very dark paint under high metal.
mistakes.fix: Use Dark Chrome 250, 15, 40, or lighten the paint a little.

mistakes.symptom: It looked great as a thumbnail and muddy on the car.
mistakes.cause: Mid-tone mud at thumbnail size stays mud on the car.
mistakes.fix: Judge on the car at a distance and on a sunny track.

protips: Test the contrast with the spec views off: if two zones are only different in shine, they will read the same in a dull photo and different in the sim.
Flat paint with chrome trim lines is the modern retro look; gloss everywhere is the showroom look.

deep.heading: Step 1: which zone owns each pixel
deep.body: Every zone builds a mask from its colour match or drawn area, softened by about 3 pixels unless the zone has a hard edge. Zones are processed in list order and an earlier zone claims first: where two overlap, the lower number wins and the later one is cut back. A soft mask above 0.15 is hardened to full ownership. At the end a zone replaces the spec fully where its mask is above 0.5, blends linearly between 0.05 and 0.5, and leaves the spot alone below that. Paint is blended by the mask in the paint stack.

deep.heading: Step 2: the paint stack inside a zone
deep.body: In order: the base finish paint (skipped when the colour mode is Use source paint, so only the spec changes); the base colour mode (solid, gradient, finish colours); hue, saturation and brightness inside the mask (hue up to 180 degrees either way, skipped if all three are under half a percent); base scale placement; then BASE STRENGTH, which mixes the result over your original paint. Patterns come after Base Strength, so lowering it never dims a pattern. Last come the second to fifth base overlays.

deep.heading: Step 3: the spec stack inside a zone
deep.body: In order: the base finish spec; SPEC STRENGTH pulling metal toward 0, roughness toward 128 and coat toward 16; base scale, rotation and clear-coat quality; a second base blended through its gradient; spec patterns (metal, roughness and coat ticks); pattern spec amount; second to fifth base overlays; then the versioned spec overlays, applied last on the finished material as a mix toward their target. After the finish is built: an imported spec map if present, spec placement, then the three SPEC sliders (R, G, B), then Material Remap, Material Override and Lighting Mask, in that order.

deep.heading: Step 4: after every zone is done
deep.body: The app protects numbers and sponsors: wherever the decal mask is on, the original colour is restored so no overlay can repaint them. Wear is applied in one pass, scaled per zone. Decal spec finishes and spec stamps are blended in by their own alpha. Then the final floors run (coat at least 16, roughness at least 15 under metal 240) and the paint and spec files are written. Preview runs exactly the same steps at a smaller size.

examples.title: Pearl body with carbon hood stripes
examples.goal: Build a layered finish and predict each layer.

settings.Spec overlay: Brushed grain, M and R ticked, Strength 50

examples.result: Pearl shimmer on gloss, a carbon weave that keeps the body colour, grain only in the shine, and a slightly softer gloss from the slider at the end.

examples.title: Overlap on purpose
examples.goal: Make a stripe beat the body where they overlap.
examples.result: The stripe is higher in the list, so it keeps the overlap. Swap the order and the body wins.

combos.why: Step 3 ends with these three sliders.
Spec Strength sits at the start of Step 3 and Base Strength at the end of Step 2. They never touch each other.
The pattern layers that sit between the base and the overlays.

faq.q: Does Base Strength change the shine?
faq.a: No. Base Strength only blends the paint toward your original colours. SPEC STRENGTH changes the shine.

faq.q: Which zone wins when two overlap?
faq.a: The one higher in the list (lower number). New zones go on top.

faq.q: What runs last, my slider or my overlay?
faq.a: The overlays run first as part of the finish, then the R, G and B sliders, then Remap, Override and Lighting Mask.

faq.q: Does the preview match the export?
faq.a: It runs the same steps and floors at a smaller size, so very fine detail can look different from the full render.

mistakes.symptom: My pattern is not dimmed when I lower Base Strength.
mistakes.cause: Patterns are added after Base Strength.
mistakes.fix: Lower the pattern opacity instead.

mistakes.symptom: A zone changes nothing.
mistakes.cause: A higher zone covers it, the colour match selects nothing, or Base Strength or intensity is low.
mistakes.fix: Check the list order, then the zone mask, then the strength sliders.

mistakes.symptom: Sponsors got a chrome look.
mistakes.cause: The body zone also grabbed the sponsor layer, and decals take the material under them.
mistakes.fix: Limit the body zone to the car paint layer and use a decal spec finish for the sponsors.

protips: Quick triage order for any odd look: zone owner, then base colour mode, then Base Strength, then SPEC STRENGTH, then the sliders.
There are at most five pattern layers and five spec overlays per zone, and each zone renders with its own random seed, so two zones with the same finish never repeat exactly.

deep.heading: Two files, two kinds of data
deep.body: The paint file is 24-bit colour, read as normal screen colour. The spec file is 32-bit with alpha and is read as raw numbers, with no colour correction. Both are 2048 by 2048 for a standard car, and the size must match the car template exactly, or iRacing shows the paint shop colours instead. An optional normal map can be written from the metal channel.

deep.heading: The compiled copy trap
deep.body: The first time iRacing loads your files it compiles the spec into a faster copy next to it. If you render again and the look does not change, that compiled copy is stale. Press Ctrl+R in the sim to reload the car textures. If the old shine still shows, move that car's compiled spec copy out of the folder and reload. Other drivers only see your spec if the compiled copy is shared too; Trading Paints shares it.

deep.heading: Byte order and tools
deep.body: The spec file stores its bytes as blue, green, red, alpha, while tools show red, green, blue, alpha. That is normal, so never swap channels by hand. Saving the spec through a photo editor can shift values, apply colour management or sharpen edges, all of which break the iron rules.

examples.title: Spec change not visible
examples.goal: Make a new render show up in the sim.

settings.If still old: Move the compiled spec copy for that car out of the folder, then Ctrl+R again

examples.result: iRacing rebuilds the compiled copy from the new spec and shows the new shine.

examples.title: Paint all black
examples.goal: Fix a paint file that loads wrong.
examples.result: The paint loads with its real colours.

combos.why: The 32-bit spec file is the one with alpha.
Editing the file elsewhere can break the rules the app enforces.

faq.q: How big must the paint be?
faq.a: Exactly 2048 by 2048 (or 1024 by 1024), 24-bit.

faq.q: Why do other drivers not see my shine?
faq.a: iRacing never shares textures. Files must be in their folder; Trading Paints does that, and its spec needs the compiled copy.

faq.q: Why is my paint all black?
faq.a: It was saved with the template alpha channel instead of 24-bit, or 2048 paint textures is off in the sim.

faq.q: Do I need the spec file at all?
faq.a: No. Without it iRacing uses the car normal material. Your colours still show.

mistakes.symptom: New shine does not show after a render.
mistakes.cause: A stale compiled copy.
mistakes.fix: Ctrl+R in the sim, or move the compiled copy out and reload.

mistakes.symptom: iRacing shows paint shop colours.
mistakes.cause: Wrong size.
mistakes.fix: Use the car template size exactly and never resize.

protips: In a replay, reload textures at a moment when the car is not in the pit stall.
A render takes seconds to about a minute. If it takes much longer, check how many zones have their own painted area.

deep.heading: The exact maths of SPEC STRENGTH
deep.body: Strength pulls the base finish toward a neutral plate: metal becomes metal times strength, roughness becomes 128 plus (roughness minus 128) times strength, coat becomes 16 plus (coat minus 16) times strength. At 100 percent nothing changes. At 50 percent Chrome (255, 2, 16) becomes about (128, 65, 16). At 0 you get metal 0, roughness 128, coat 16, a neutral gloss. It runs on the base spec before patterns and overlays, so those keep their own strength.

deep.heading: Three strengths that are easy to mix up
deep.body: SPEC STRENGTH changes the shine and leaves colour alone. BASE STRENGTH blends the base paint over your original paint and leaves the spec alone. INTENSITY scales how strong a base texture generator is. Use the right one: less shiny means SPEC STRENGTH, more subtle colour means BASE STRENGTH or intensity, smaller pattern means scale, not strength.

deep.heading: Independent spec
deep.body: By default the spec texture follows the base scale and rotation, so a brushed grain turns with the brushed paint. Tick INDEPENDENT SPEC to unlock SPEC SCALE and SPEC ROTATION so the shine texture can be finer, larger or turned differently from the paint. Only the spec moves; the colour stays put.

examples.title: Half-chrome
examples.goal: A softer chrome look without changing finish.
examples.result: Metal about 128 and roughness about 65: a bright metallic with soft reflections instead of a mirror.

examples.title: Grain across the paint grain
examples.goal: Turn the shine texture 45 degrees from the paint texture.
examples.result: The spec grain is finer and diagonal to the base texture.

combos.why: The two controls that Independent Spec unlocks.
Where Spec Strength sits in the order of operations.
Sliders add after strength; use strength for overall, sliders for one channel.

faq.q: Does strength 0 mean dull?
faq.a: No. It is neutral: metal 0, roughness 128, coat 16, a plain gloss. Coat 16 is the glossiest coat.

faq.q: Which slider makes the car less shiny?
faq.a: SPEC STRENGTH, or G ROUGH plus 40.

faq.q: Does strength change colour?
faq.a: No. Only the spec.

faq.q: Why can I not change SPEC SCALE?
faq.a: It is locked until INDEPENDENT SPEC is ticked.

mistakes.symptom: Lowering strength made the car look like plain gloss.
mistakes.cause: Strength pulls toward a neutral plate, so every finish converges on plain gloss at 0.
mistakes.fix: Lower in small steps, or change the base finish.

mistakes.symptom: I used strength to shrink a pattern.
mistakes.cause: Strength is not size.
mistakes.fix: Use scale. Smaller number means finer and more repeats.

protips: Authored imports (SHOKK DROP sets) ignore SPEC STRENGTH on purpose, so their hand-tuned numbers stay exact.
The same slider also scales the noise in noisy bases, so on those the effect is a bit stronger than the plain formula.

deep.heading: What scale really does on a whole car
deep.body: The canvas is 2048 by 2048 and covers the entire car. A feature of 8 to 32 pixels reads as texture; 64 pixels is the size of a side mirror. Scale runs from 0.05 to 5 times with 1.00 as the finish default, and smaller means more repeats, so 0.30 to 0.60 is typical for fine detail. The app also auto-scales a pattern to the zone size: 1.0 if the zone covers more than 60 percent of the canvas, otherwise about the square root of its area share, between 0.15 and 1.

deep.heading: Spec placement is its own pass
deep.body: After the zone finish is built, a separate placement pass moves, turns, scales and flips only the spec. That is why independent spec scale and rotation never recolour anything. Rotation goes 0 to 355 degrees in steps of 5.

deep.heading: The fine-detail rule
deep.body: Fine is 4 to 8 pixels, micro is 1 to 2 pixels (car-scale sparkle), and 8 to 32 pixels is the sweet spot for a finish that reads as material. When detail seems enough, make it 25 to 40 percent finer. If a finish does not show up, add more small events and more channel contrast; do not make the marks bigger.

examples.title: Brushed grain that reads as steel
examples.goal: Fine, horizontal brushing on a hood.
examples.result: Twice as many grain lines across the hood, the size of real brushing at distance.

examples.title: Carbon on the diagonal
examples.goal: Turn a weave without turning the paint.
examples.result: The weave in the spec runs diagonally while any painted pattern stays put.

combos.why: The paint version of the same idea. Pattern scale is a separate control.
Independent spec must be ticked first.

faq.q: Why is my texture huge?
faq.a: Scale 1.00 on a whole-car canvas is often too big. Go to 0.3 to 0.6.

faq.q: Does spec scale change the paint?
faq.a: No. Spec only.

faq.q: What is the best size?
faq.a: Features of 8 to 32 pixels at 2048.

faq.q: Does rotation work on flat finishes?
faq.a: There is nothing to turn on a flat spec. It needs a texture, such as brushed grain or a weave.

mistakes.symptom: Scale is greyed out.
mistakes.cause: INDEPENDENT SPEC is not ticked.
mistakes.fix: Tick it first.

mistakes.symptom: Fine detail disappears in the preview.
mistakes.cause: The preview is smaller than the 2048 export.
mistakes.fix: Zoom in or read the spec views before deciding it did nothing.

protips: Preview is about 768 pixels for a 2048 sheet. Micro flake and holographic grating at small scale average out and look flat there.
Rotation of 45 degrees on a weave is the quickest way to a different carbon look.

deep.heading: Exactly what a slider does
deep.body: Each slider adds its value, from minus 127 to plus 127, to that channel under the zone mask. The result is clipped at 0 to 255, with floors of 0 for metal, 15 for roughness and 16 for coat. Sliders at 0 (or all under half a point) are ignored. The sliders run after patterns, overlays and blend modes, so they are the last creative step; only Remap, Override and Lighting Mask come after.

deep.heading: Which way each one goes
deep.body: Metal plus means more metal. Roughness plus means duller, minus means glossier. Coat plus means duller, because blue is backwards, minus means glossier and stops at 16. Rough recipes: satin from gloss is G ROUGH plus 40 to plus 80 with B COAT plus 30 to plus 60. Wetter is G ROUGH minus and B COAT minus.

deep.heading: Sliders versus other tools
deep.body: Sliders shift a whole zone evenly. Material Remap squeezes a channel into a new low to high range and keeps variation. Material Override sets flat values. Spec Strength pulls everything toward neutral. A shift of 20 is subtle, 50 is a clear style change, and anything near 100 usually cancels the finish character.

examples.title: Satin from gloss
examples.goal: Take a gloss body to satin without changing the base.
examples.result: Roughness around 90 and coat around 61: a quiet satin.

examples.title: Duller candy
examples.goal: Take some wet depth out of a candy zone.
examples.result: Roughness 45 and coat 36: the candy colour stays but the glassy look relaxes into a satin candy.

combos.why: Feels are slider combinations saved as one click.
The tools that run right after the sliders.
The floors that clip slider results.

faq.q: Why does B COAT plus make it duller?
faq.a: Because blue is backwards. The number is added to the coat value, where bigger means less coat.

faq.q: Why did my slider stop working?
faq.a: The channel reached its floor or ceiling.

faq.q: Can sliders recolour?
faq.a: No. They only change metal, roughness and coat.

faq.q: Slider or SPEC STRENGTH?
faq.a: Use the slider to move one channel. Use strength to scale the whole finish.

mistakes.symptom: Large shifts make the finish look generic.
mistakes.cause: A shift near 100 overwhelms the base values.
mistakes.fix: Choose a different base finish and nudge by 20 to 40.

mistakes.symptom: Wetter did not work on a gel coat.
mistakes.cause: It is already at the floor of 15 and 16.
mistakes.fix: Nothing more to gain. Change the pattern or the paint.

protips: The B COAT slider tooltip in the app says higher is a stronger mirror. The number is really added to the coat value where bigger means duller, so judge by eye.
Save a good slider set as a Feel so it can be reused on other zones.

deep.heading: The order the three tools run
deep.body: After the sliders, the zone spec goes through Material Remap first, then Material Override, then Lighting Mask. All three run before the final floors, so a flat override of roughness 5 on a non-chrome pixel is lifted to 15 and a coat of 1 to 15 is lifted to 16. Remap and Override work per channel (metal, roughness, coat); Lighting Mask only touches alpha.

deep.heading: Remap in numbers
deep.body: Remap squeezes a channel into a new low and high range: result = low + source / 255 times (high minus low). A source 0 goes to Low and a source 255 goes to High. A metal range of 0 to 100 turns a chrome (255) into metal 100 but keeps every bit of variation, so a brushed grain stays brushed while the whole thing calms down. Override is blunt: it sets one flat value for the channel across the zone and loses all variation.

deep.heading: Sampler and decal rescue
deep.body: The Material Sampler reads the exact metal, roughness and coat at a spot (Point, 3 by 3 median or 5 by 5 median) and can copy them onto the active zone. Decal Rescue Kit puts a plain non-metal spec under stamped numbers and sponsors: Flat Vinyl, Satin Decal or Gloss Decal, so they do not take the sparkle of whatever spec is below.

examples.title: Calm a too-sparkly metallic
examples.goal: Keep the texture, lower the metal.
examples.result: The brightest flakes now peak at metal 120 and every pattern shape is still there.

examples.title: Rescue sponsor logos
examples.goal: Stop numbers and sponsors from going sparkly under chrome.

settings.Body zone: Limited to the car paint layer

examples.result: Decals keep a plain non-metal look while the body stays chrome.

combos.why: Sliders run just before these tools, so a remap or override can overrule a slider.
Lighting Mask is the tool that changes alpha.
The floors run after all three tools.

faq.q: Remap or slider?
faq.a: Sliders move the whole zone evenly. Remap rescales the range and keeps the variation.

faq.q: Can I undo a remap?
faq.a: Yes. Restore Original puts the zone back.

faq.q: What does Override do to texture?
faq.a: It flattens the channel to one value, so texture in that channel is lost.

faq.q: Do these tools change colour?
faq.a: No. They only change spec channels and alpha.

mistakes.symptom: My override of coat 5 became 16.
mistakes.cause: The floors run after the tools.
mistakes.fix: Use 16 or more.

mistakes.symptom: Override removed my brushed grain.
mistakes.cause: A flat value replaces the channel.
mistakes.fix: Use Remap, which keeps variation.

mistakes.symptom: Numbers look sparkly or dull.
mistakes.cause: Stamped items take the spec of whatever is under them.
mistakes.fix: Use Decal Rescue Kit and limit the body zone to the car paint layer.

protips: Remap presets are a fast start: Original, Metallic Texture, Printed Vinyl, Matte Texture and Gloss Texture. Then fine tune Low and High.
Use the Material Sampler first. Copying exact numbers from a part you like is quicker than guessing.

deep.heading: The six named modes rewrite three channels
deep.body: Ghost Carve pulls the coat value toward 64 plus 176 times the pattern, so pattern lows and highs land at very different coat values and form carved cells, and lowers roughness by up to 25. It leaves the metal alone, so any base keeps its tinted flash. Chrome Inlay lowers metal (by up to 85 percent) and roughness (by up to 65 percent) where the pattern is hot and pushes the coat value toward 245: a mirror inlay in a metal surround. Frost Etch lowers metal by up to 45, raises roughness by up to 150 and lowers the coat value by up to 35: sandblasted, milky areas. Angle Flip adds up to plus or minus 85 metal and moves the coat value by the opposite sign, up to 135, so the pattern shows at one angle and inverts at another. Ember Gate lights only the top ridges: above a pattern value of 0.80 the coat value goes to 252 and roughness to 34. Depth Press embosses: a lit rim (metal plus 110, coat plus 90) and a shadow rim (metal minus 70).

deep.heading: Without a pattern the zone itself is the field
deep.body: These modes work with or without a pattern. With a pattern the pattern drives the effect. Without one, the zone's own paint structure drives it, so your livery becomes the carve: the field is the paint brightness first, the base spec shape second, a flat 0.5 last. Flat solid zones with a featureless base respond only subtly, so give the mode some structure to work with.

deep.heading: The legacy five
deep.body: Multiply, Screen, Overlay, Hard Light and Soft Light are the older blend modes that mix the overlay values with the base. They keep working but can wash out a finish, and a strong overlay under a classic mode may flatten it. The named modes are physical: they change how metal, gloss and coat behave, not just brightness. All modes honour the iron floors afterward.

examples.title: Carve a livery into chrome
examples.goal: Make the livery shapes read as mirror cuts.
examples.result: Hot parts of the pattern become mirror-like inlays while the surround loses most of its metal.

examples.title: Colour-flip from any base
examples.goal: Get angle-dependent flashes on a dark colour.
examples.result: Cells with different coat values flash sky or sun colour as the car turns, while the metal stays tinted and dark.

combos.why: Ghost Carve is the recipe behind most angle-reveal finishes.
Blend decides how an overlay meets the base; the stack decides the order.
See where the blend sits in the order of operations.

faq.q: Which mode for sparkle that ignites on edges?
faq.a: Ember Gate. Only the brightest ridges light up.

faq.q: Which mode for a stamped look?
faq.a: Depth Press. Every element gets a lit rim and a shadow rim.

faq.q: Why does nothing change on my plain zone?
faq.a: Flat solid zones with featureless bases respond subtly. Add a pattern or a structured base.

faq.q: Do the modes change the colour?
faq.a: No. They change metal, roughness and coat only.

mistakes.symptom: The effect is too strong and everything is chrome.
mistakes.cause: Strength and pattern spec amount both high with Chrome Inlay.
mistakes.fix: Lower strength before the next layer.

mistakes.symptom: Ghost Carve shows nothing.
mistakes.cause: The base colour is too bright, so diffuse colour hides the flashes.
mistakes.fix: Crush the colour near black and judge on a daytime track.

mistakes.symptom: A classic blend washed out my finish.
mistakes.cause: Legacy modes mix values directly.
mistakes.fix: Switch to a named mode or lower strength.

protips: Compare Normal and the named mode side by side before you commit.
Angle Flip is the one to try for a finish that changes between camera angles in replays.

deep.heading: How an overlay changes the spec
deep.body: Each spec overlay moves the finished material toward its own target on the channels you tick (M, R, C): result = current + (target minus current) times coverage times strength. Strength defaults to 50 percent. Overlays are applied last on the finished material, so the base cannot undo them, and the later sliders and floors still apply afterward.

deep.heading: Order and channels
deep.body: The stack runs from the first layer to the fifth, each mixing onto the result of the one before. Texture on roughness only is the safest: it changes how light spreads without touching metal or the coat. M-only overlays add sparkle on metal. C-only overlays vary the clearcoat and tend to be the most visible in direct sun. Five layers at full strength fight each other, so build with two or three and balance their strengths.

deep.heading: Debugging a busy look
deep.body: Mute turns a layer off without deleting it and Solo shows only that layer. Inspect reads the numbers at a spot. Because spec overlays never change colour, a flat colour preview looks identical with and without them. Use the spec views (R METAL, G ROUGH, B COAT) or the Channels readout to confirm they did anything.

examples.title: Brushed steel hood
examples.goal: Real brushed texture on a metallic base.
examples.result: Fine directional grain with occasional bright glints.

examples.title: Carbon under gloss
examples.goal: Visible weave only in the shine.
examples.result: A weave that moves with the light while the paint stays a plain colour.

combos.why: The blend mode changes how each overlay meets the base spec.
Where to find each kind of overlay.
Paint patterns and spec overlays both stack to five, but only patterns change colour.

faq.q: How many overlays can I stack?
faq.a: Up to five per zone.

faq.q: Why does my overlay do nothing in the preview?
faq.a: Overlays change shine only. Check the spec views.

faq.q: What strength should I use?
faq.a: Start at 50, the default, and go lower if the look is loud. 30 to 50 reads as subtle flake.

faq.q: Can I mute a layer?
faq.a: Yes. Mute, Solo and Duplicate are on each layer.

mistakes.symptom: Everything looks noisy.
mistakes.cause: Several overlays at high strength on all three channels.
mistakes.fix: Solo each layer, tick fewer channels, lower strength.

mistakes.symptom: The old stack disappeared.
mistakes.cause: Setting overlays through an apply command replaces the stack.
mistakes.fix: Add layers one at a time with Add Spec Overlay.

protips: A subtle flake overlay at strength 30 to 50 adds depth to almost any finish.
Pick the channel on purpose. The same pattern on R, on M and on C gives three different looks.

deep.heading: What each Feel really does
deep.body: A Feel is three slider values applied at once, each between minus 127 and plus 127. Wet Candy is metal plus 30, roughness minus 55, coat plus 45. Track Flash is 55, minus 35, plus 60. Chrome Mirror is 80, minus 80, plus 70. Deep Gloss is 25, minus 45, plus 85. Soft Pearl is 15, 25, 10. Satin Matte is minus 25, plus 65, minus 15. Roughness minus always means glossier. The coat numbers are positive, and because the coat byte is backwards a plus value makes the coat duller, so these Feels make the coat a little duller while they lower roughness and add metal.

deep.heading: Feels sit on top of the finish
deep.body: They are added to whatever the finish already is, then clipped at 0 for metal, 15 for roughness and 16 for coat. So Chrome Mirror on a matte finish will not make it chrome: metal 0 plus 80 and roughness 200 minus 80 is a satin metal. On a gloss finish the same Feel makes a real step toward chrome.

deep.heading: Your own Feels
deep.body: Set the three sliders, click the save icon, and the Feel is kept on this computer next to the built-in ones. They are not shared with other computers or other drivers.

examples.title: Candy glow
examples.goal: More wet depth on a coloured gloss.
examples.result: Roughness drops and metal rises a little for a deeper, glassier colour.

examples.title: Quick stealth
examples.goal: Turn a gloss zone into a flat one.
examples.result: Roughness 30 plus 65 is 95 and coat 16 minus 15 clips at 16: a satin from gloss in one click.

combos.why: A Feel is just three slider values; fine tune them by hand afterward.
Auto-Pop is the automatic version of a Feel.

faq.q: Do Feels change colour?
faq.a: No.

faq.q: Can I stack two Feels?
faq.a: A Feel sets the sliders, so a second one replaces the first.

faq.q: Where are saved Feels kept?
faq.a: On this computer only.

faq.q: Which Feel for chrome?
faq.a: Chrome Mirror, but start from a gloss or metallic base. On a matte base it will only reach satin metal.

mistakes.symptom: A Feel did nothing on chrome.
mistakes.cause: The finish was already at the limit of the channels the Feel pushes.
mistakes.fix: Pick a Feel that pushes the other way.

mistakes.symptom: The coat looks duller with Wet Candy.
mistakes.cause: Its coat number is positive and the coat scale is backwards.
mistakes.fix: Judge by eye and lower B COAT by 5s if you want it wetter.

protips: Apply a Feel, then fine tune in steps of 5.
Feels are a good way to learn the sliders: apply one and look at what the R, G and B values became.

deep.heading: The exact thresholds
deep.body: Auto-Pop reads the zone average from the spec preview. If the metal average is under 70 it adds up to 15 metal, 30 percent of the gap to 70. If roughness averages over 70 it lowers roughness by the excess, up to 45. If the coat averages over 55 it lowers the coat value by the excess, up to 45, which is glossier. Every step is a multiple of 5 and it only moves in the direction of gloss. A zone that is already glossy gets a note and no change.

deep.heading: What it needs and what it does not do
deep.body: It needs a spec preview to have been rendered first, because it measures the real zone spec. It adds to the three sliders, so it can be undone in one step. It will not turn matte into chrome, because the metal boost is capped at 15 and roughness and coat drop by at most 45 per click. Repeated clicks keep boosting until the limits are reached.

examples.title: Rescue a dull zone
examples.goal: Add life to a zone that renders flat.
examples.result: The sliders move by a few steps toward more metal and less roughness. Check the car and press Undo if it is not right.

examples.title: Already glossy
examples.goal: See that Auto-Pop respects a good zone.
examples.result: It says the zone is already glossy and changes nothing.

combos.why: Auto-Pop moves these three sliders.
For a bigger, deliberate move use a Feel.

faq.q: Will Auto-Pop wreck my finish?
faq.a: No. It is small, conservative, and one Undo step.

faq.q: Why does it ask me to render first?
faq.a: It measures the real spec preview of the zone.

faq.q: Does it add colour?
faq.a: No. Spec only.

faq.q: Can I use it twice?
faq.a: Yes, each click boosts again until the limits.

mistakes.symptom: Nothing happened.
mistakes.cause: The zone is already glossy, or no spec preview was rendered.
mistakes.fix: Render a preview first and read the message.

mistakes.symptom: I wanted a matte car shiny.
mistakes.cause: Auto-Pop is capped at gentle steps.
mistakes.fix: Use a Feel or choose a different base finish.

protips: Auto-Pop is a safe first move when a zone looks dull and you do not know why.
After Auto-Pop the sliders hold real numbers, so you can read them to learn what the zone needed.

deep.heading: Seeing the real numbers
deep.body: The Material Sampler shows exact metal, roughness, coat and alpha at a clicked spot. The channel buttons ALL, R, G, B and A switch the preview between the channels. Sample modes are Point, 3 by 3 Median and 5 by 5 Median, and a table lists the minimum, maximum and mean of each channel. Use Median on any textured area, because a single point on grain gives a random value.

deep.heading: Finding and copying a material
deep.body: Select Connected grows from the clicked pixel across touching similar pixels; Select All Similar finds every matching pixel on the car. Material tolerance runs from 0 to 64 with a default of 12. Copy M, R, CC and A copy the numbers, and Apply to Active Zone writes them as an override for the zone. Clear Zone Override undoes it.

deep.heading: The material readout
deep.body: After a preview renders, the app also reports the material mix of the whole spec as a bar: percent glossy, metallic and matte, with plain warnings for flat or whitewashed settings, such as coat in the 1 to 15 dead band or a metal floor too low. Treat it as a quick check before you export.

faq.q: Why does the same finish read different values?
faq.a: Textured finishes vary. Use Median sampling and compare means.

faq.q: Is the Sampler changing my car?
faq.a: Not until you press Apply to Active Zone.

faq.q: What tolerance should I use?
faq.a: 12 is the default. Raise it to find broader areas.

faq.q: Does it show the preview or the export?
faq.a: The preview spec. The export runs the same steps at full size.

mistakes.symptom: Values jump between clicks.
mistakes.cause: Point sampling on a textured area.
mistakes.fix: Switch to a Median size.

mistakes.symptom: Select All Similar grabbed too much.
mistakes.cause: Tolerance too high.
mistakes.fix: Lower it toward 12 or less.

protips: Sample the spot you like, copy the numbers, then recreate it with a base and sliders. You learn what makes it.
Bright green in the spec colour views means rough, not shiny.

deep.heading: The mechanism in three lobes
deep.body: There is no true colour rotation in the sim. What exists is paint-tinted metal, environment-coloured clear coat and roughness gating. Metal at 176 to 255 keeps the reflection tinted with the paint hue even when the paint is nearly black. The clear coat is a separate, nearly white lobe that mirrors the environment: teal sky at one angle, gold sun or tarmac at another. Crushing the base colour removes the diffuse light, so only the two lobes remain and cells flip between dark and flash as the car turns.

deep.heading: What it needs to read
deep.body: Two cell styles work: large coherent cells (the Ghost Shift recipe) and fine cells of 8 to 32 pixels whose channels disagree (the Fractured and ColorShoxx style). For the fine style use 6 to 8 crushed near-black shades (about 10 to 18 percent lightness) so metal cells cross lighting thresholds at different times. A single flat magenta carrier looks dead. Two routes work: a dark buried palette (any hue, best for warm, green and copper) or a bright cool base (blue, violet, magenta). Warm bright bases blend into warm sun and lose the second colour.

deep.heading: Where to judge it
deep.body: Flash colours come from the track's sky and sun, so daytime tracks show them best and night or indoor lighting mutes them. Judge on the curved hood, roof and fenders, because a flat door can hold the base look longer. A good one reveals panel by panel, not the whole car at once, and survives shade, glare and replay distance.

The finish families built on this idea.
Fractured carriers sit in a corner of the grid with metal 242 to 255.

faq.q: Can paint really change colour with the angle?
faq.a: Not with a true shader. Colour-shift finishes fake it with paint plus spec.

faq.q: Why does the effect disappear at night?
faq.a: The flash colours come from the sky and sun; night mutes them.

faq.q: Why dark colours?
faq.a: A bright paint adds diffuse light that hides the two specular lobes.

faq.q: Does the preview show it?
faq.a: The flat preview cannot show angle changes. Judge it in the sim on a daytime track.

mistakes.symptom: It reads as sparkle, not a shift.
mistakes.cause: Pins or cells too large or all one shade.
mistakes.fix: Use finer cells and 6 to 8 dark shades.

mistakes.symptom: The second colour never shows.
mistakes.cause: A warm bright base blended into warm sun.
mistakes.fix: Use a dark buried palette, or a cool bright base.

mistakes.symptom: Hot pink spec did not flip.
mistakes.cause: Pink is only how the bytes pack. The effect needs spatial pattern, dark paint and lighting.
mistakes.fix: Add the pattern and crush the paint.

protips: Offset the clear-coat structure from the metal structure so the two lobes peak at different angles.
Judge on a daytime track and on the hood and fenders, not on a flat door.

deep.heading: How the 301 are organised
deep.body: The picker sorts spec patterns into groups by what the texture does: sparkle and micro-metal, optical and interference, directional metal and brush, carbon and composite weave, clearcoat and coating, structure and geometry, surface and spray texture, weather and wear, machined hardware, and themed sets such as predator skins, voodoo, rising sun and let freedom ring. Source Pattern Plates is the largest group with 24 and matches the plate finishes of the same name.

deep.heading: Choosing by job
deep.body: Want sparkle or flake: the Sparkle and Micro-Metal group. Want weave: Carbon and Composite Weave. Want brushed or machined: Directional Metal and Brush, Machined and Race Hardware. Want rainbow or oil film: Optical and Interference, or a holographic overlay over a pearl, metallic or chrome base. Want worn or weathered: Weather, Wear and Track plus a rougher base. Themed groups are loud, so lower strength before stacking another layer.

deep.heading: Every one changes shine only
deep.body: Each spec pattern lists which channels it touches by default (M, R or C) and you can tick or untick them. Roughness only is the safest choice for subtle texture.

faq.q: Which group first?
faq.a: Sparkle and Micro-Metal and Carbon and Composite Weave are the safest first picks.

faq.q: Why do some groups look the same?
faq.a: They are different names for related textures; compare them on the spec views.

faq.q: Can I search instead?
faq.a: Yes. The picker has search.

faq.q: Do spec patterns match the paint patterns?
faq.a: Source Pattern Plates match the plate finishes of the same name.

mistakes.symptom: A themed group looks too loud.
mistakes.cause: Strength 50 is strong for a bold texture.
mistakes.fix: Lower strength before adding a second layer.

mistakes.symptom: I cannot see the pattern.
mistakes.cause: Spec patterns change shine only.
mistakes.fix: Check the spec views and the sim.

protips: A holographic overlay needs a reflective base. On matte paint it has nothing to shimmer.
Try the same pattern on R only, then on C only. The look changes more than the pattern does.
